name_or_item: LYR four-cylinder compound vs two-cylinder simple sister engines (ten of each, built 1907)
source_ref: G. Hughes, 'Compounding and Superheating in Horwich Locomotives', Proc. IMechE 1910 vol. 78 p. 399, discussion at p. 456. https://www.lyrs.org.uk/images/uploads/Paper_-_Hughes_1910_-_I.Mech.E_-_Compounding_and_Superheating_in_Horwich_Locomotives.pdf
notes: Average first cost of the ten new compounds was GBP 260 per engine more than ten new sister simples. Hughes states boilers, steam pressures, grate areas, heating surfaces, valve motions and wheels were 'exactly the same in both instances', so this is a true matched pair. Computed as a percentage on an assumed GBP 2,500-3,500 base = 7 to 10 per cent; the paper does not state the base price.

name_or_item: LYR superheated vs non-superheated engines (twenty of each, otherwise identical)
source_ref: G. Hughes, Proc. IMechE 1910 vol. 78 p. 456, as above
notes: 'The actual average extra cost of twenty new superheater over twenty new non-superheater engines was GBP 350 per engine.' Same paper, same works, same year, engines otherwise identical. On an assumed GBP 2,500-3,500 base = 10 to 14 per cent.

name_or_item: LYR superheater, expected cost for future lots
source_ref: G. Hughes, Proc. IMechE 1910 vol. 78 p. 456, as above
notes: Hughes: 'future lots of engines could be built for GBP 300 per engine extra'. Forward-looking statement by the chief mechanical engineer, not an outturn.

name_or_item: LBSCR cost of fitting superheating (Marsh, in discussion)
source_ref: D. E. Marsh, contribution to the discussion, Proc. IMechE 1910 vol. 78 pp. 469-70, as above
notes: Marsh said superheating 'had been done on the Brighton Railway for about half that amount', i.e. about half of Hughes's GBP 350. The paper elsewhere gives 'the figure of GBP 175 capital cost, as given by Mr. Marsh'. Cheapest British figure found; conversion of existing engines, not new build.

name_or_item: High-degree superheater conversion parts, excluding cylinders (quoted for an overseas railway)
source_ref: Proc. IMechE 1910 vol. 78 pp. 470-1 (Cowan and discussion), as above
notes: 'The new parts, as recommended by the owners of one of the high-degree systems of superheating ... cost over GBP 600', of which GBP 300 was new cylinders and gear. Conversion kit, not a new-build premium; upper bound.

name_or_item: Trevithick smoke-box superheater conversion parts (quoted for an overseas railway)
source_ref: Proc. IMechE 1910 vol. 78 p. 470, as above
notes: 'The cost of the new parts required by the Trevithick system ... amounted to less than GBP 100'. Low-degree system; the lower bound of the conversion range.

name_or_item: Worsdell-von Borries two-cylinder compound vs two-cylinder simple of equal tractive effort
source_ref: E. M. Gass, 'The Application of the Compound Principle to Locomotives', Paper 208, Institution of Locomotive Engineers, 29 October 1926, p. 25 (author's reply). https://www.lyrs.org.uk/images/uploads/Paper_-_Gass_1927_-_I.Loco.E_-_The_Application_of_the_Compound_Principle_to_Locomotives.pdf
notes: 'The Worsdell von-Borries compound cost approximately GBP 200 more to build than the single expansion engine', the two having the same tractive power. Compound added to a two-cylinder layout; the comparison is of an earlier generation of engines reported in 1926.

name_or_item: Four-cylinder compound vs four-cylinder simple of equal capacity (French practice reported to the I.Loco.E.)
source_ref: E. M. Gass, Paper 208, 1926, p. 25, as above
notes: Gass: 'the four-cylinder compound locomotive with only two sets of valve gear cost practically the same to build as the four-cylinder single expansion engine'. Key result: at constant cylinder count the compounding itself carried no measurable first-cost premium; the cost sits in cylinders and valve gear.
